data.content_ref: inline:exp-hist:{"target": "feb16caec9d21850adcc448ff37baee93a74ce6e0f6d5de1ef79dc64e282eb78", "seq": 1, "objection": "The argument fails on Popper's own terms because the preference for a theory that has 'withstood high-content attacks' in the past to minimize future error risk is functionally identical to the inductive principle it claims to reject. Popper explicitly denied that past survival makes a theory more probable or reliable for the future; therefore, acting on the basis that a well-corroborated theory is a safer bet for future application smuggles in the very assumption that nature is uniform (that past performance predicts future stability). The target asserts this is merely a 'strategic choice based on logical structure,' but the utility of that strategy depends entirely on the inductive hope that the conditions which allowed falsification in the past will remain operative in the future. Without this inductive bridge, the 'cost of error' calculation is groundless, as a highly corroborated theory has no logical guarantee of not failing immediately upon the next test.", "outcome": "raised and not answered; the target's status did not move"}
